skills-scale-s1.title: Homes with internet access by province, Country A (national average: 60%)

map.label: Shaded map of the eight provinces of Country A: internet access is highest in the Capital Region and the Lake District and lowest in the Western Uplands and the Southern Forest

items.q: What is the scale of analysis of the data on this map?
options: Local (subnational): one value for each province
National: the map shows the whole of one country
Global: the data could be compared with other countries
Regional: Country A counts as a region of the world

why.correct: Ask what unit each number describes. Each shade is one province, so the scale of analysis is local (subnational), not national.
options: Right: the scale of analysis is set by the unit each value describes. Here that unit is a province, a part of the country.
This is the common slip. The map covers one country, but each shade describes one province, so the data are subnational.
Global data would have values for countries across the world. This map has values for provinces in one country.
The regional scale is a group of countries. Each value here is for one province inside one country.

items.q: The title gives one national figure: 60% of homes have internet access. What does the map show that the national figure hides?
options: Access is about 60% in each province, just as the national figure says
Access is 80% or more in the Capital Region but under 40% in the Western Uplands
Country A has more homes with internet than its neighbors have
Access is rising faster in the Western Uplands than it is in the Capital Region these days

why.correct: One national number can hide large differences between provinces. Reading the data at a smaller scale shows them.
options: The shades run from under 40% to 80% or more, so the provinces are far from equal.
Right: a national average blends high and low provinces into one number. The map shows the gap.
The map counts no homes and shows no other country.
A rise needs data from two dates. This map shows one date.

items.q: Country A's government can build new internet lines in two provinces this year. Which data should it use to choose them, and why?
options: The national figure of 60%, because one number is easier to compare with other countries
A world map of internet access, because it covers the most land and the most countries
The province data, because they show access is lowest in the Western Uplands and Southern Forest
The province data, because the Capital Region has the highest access of any province

why.correct: Match the scale of the data to the scale of the decision: a choice between provinces needs data by province.
options: The national figure gives one number for the whole country, so it cannot rank the provinces.
A world map would show Country A as a single value and hide its provinces.
Right: the choice is between provinces, so the data must be for provinces.
The province data are the right scale, but the highest access is where new lines are needed least.

items.q: A world map is shaded so that each country has one color for its share of people living in cities. What is the scale of analysis of its data?
options: Global: the map shows the whole world
Local: cities are measured
Regional: the countries are grouped into world regions
National: there is one value for each country

why.correct: The scale of analysis is the unit of the data (here, countries), not the size of the area the map covers.
options: The map's size is the world, but the unit each value describes is a country.
The measure is about cities, but each value is a share for a whole country.
No values are given for groups of countries; each country has its own.
Right: each value describes one country, even though the map covers the world.

items.q: On a map with a scale of 1:50,000, two villages are 4 cm apart. How far apart are they on the ground, in kilometers?

mistakes.why: That is the distance in centimeters (4 x 50,000). Divide by 100,000 to turn centimeters into kilometers.
A factor of 10 off: 100,000 cm make 1 km, so 200,000 cm is 2 km, not 20 km.

why.correct: $4 \times 50{,}000 = 200{,}000$ cm on the ground, and $\frac{200{,}000}{100{,}000} = 2$ km, because 100,000 cm make 1 km.

items.q: Which map is the large-scale map?
options: A map of one neighborhood at 1:5,000
A map of the world at 1:100,000,000
A map of a continent at 1:20,000,000
A map of a large country at 1:10,000,000

why.correct: In map scale, "large scale" means the fraction 1:denominator is large, so features look large and the area shown is small. It is the opposite of what the words suggest.
options: Right: 1:5,000 is the biggest fraction, so things look large and the map shows a small area in detail.
This is the smallest fraction, so it is the smallest-scale map: a large area with little detail.
A continent at 1:20,000,000 is a small-scale map: things look tiny.
A whole country at 1:10,000,000 is a small-scale map, even though the country is large.

items.q: Put the four scales of analysis in order, from the largest area to the smallest.
options: Global scale
Regional scale
National scale
Local scale

why.correct: Global covers the world, regional a group of countries (such as South Asia), national one country, and local a part of a country (a province, city or neighborhood).

items.q: A student writes: "A large-scale map shows a large area, like the whole world." Which correction is right?
options: A large-scale map shows a medium area, such as one country, with average detail
A large-scale map shows a small area, such as a town, in great detail
A large-scale map covers more ground than a small-scale map does
A large-scale map shows data at the global scale of analysis, not the local

why.correct: Map scale is a ratio. A large-scale map has a large fraction (like 1:5,000), so it shows a small area in detail.
options: Map scale is about the fraction, not a middle size. A country map is usually small scale.
Right: large scale means a large fraction (1:5,000), so the area is small and the detail is high.
This repeats the student's mistake: a small-scale map covers more ground.
Map scale and scale of analysis are different ideas; a large-scale map can show local data.

items.q: Build a sentence that names the scale of analysis of the Country A internet map and what it shows.

specific.frame: At the ___ scale, the data show that ___.
specific.model: At the local (subnational) scale, the data show that internet access is 80% or more in the Capital Region but under 40% in the Western Uplands of Country A.

scale.label: Scale of analysis
options: local (subnational)
national
global

why.1: The map shows one country, but each value is for a province: that is local (subnational) data.
why.2: Global data would give values for many countries; these are provinces of one country.

pattern.label: Pattern with places
options: access is highest in the Capital Region and lowest in the Western Uplands
access varies
access is 60% across Country A

why.1: Too vague to earn credit: say where it is high and where it is low.
why.2: 60% is the national average; the map shows provinces far above and below it.

why.correct: Name the scale from the unit of the data (provinces), then name the places at each end of the pattern.

items.q: Egypt's national figure for people per square kilometer is moderate, yet almost all Egyptians live in the Nile valley and delta. What does this show about scale?
options: National data for Egypt are wrong, so the national figure should be thrown out
Egypt's people are spread evenly across the valley, the delta and the desert
A pattern can change with scale: the national figure hides a crowded valley and an empty desert
The national figure is more accurate than local data, so it settles the question

why.correct: A single national number blends very different places. Looking at the local scale shows the real pattern: crowded along the Nile, nearly empty in the desert.
options: National data are useful for comparing countries; they hide differences inside a country.
The question says the opposite: people live in the valley and delta, not across the desert.
Right: averaging the crowded valley with the nearly empty desert gives a moderate number that describes neither.
Neither scale is more accurate; each answers a different question.
